title: Lob Game
aim: Hit an overhead with the same motion as a throw, lob only off a ball you can attack, and play the lob-against-overhead duel at the kitchen line.

stages.title: Throw It Down
stages.inShort: A tosses high balls, and B throws them down by hand first, then hits the same motion with the paddle as an overhead.
rules: An overhead is a hard shot hit from above your head, like a tennis serve. B stands near the baseline. A tosses slow, high, predictable balls to B.
First without paddles: B uses the empty hand and the natural throwing motion. Step, pull the elbow back, reach up, throw down.
The elbow and the feet move at the same time.
Then with the paddle in the throwing hand: A plays high balls, and B keeps the same order: elbow back, reach up, hit down.
Point your free hand at the ball. That gives you the distance and gets you to hit high and in front.
stages.tooEasy: A mixes the depth and pace: one step for a near ball, two or more for a deep one. Even harder: A now and then tosses a wrong ball (too short or too deep), and B decides: overhead or reset (a soft ball back).
stages.tooHard: Stay longer without the paddle, until the throwing motion and the footwork work together.
stages.goodLooksLike: Contact high and in front, the free arm stays up, and the paddle finishes across to the opposite hip.

stages.title: Lob Over the Paddle
stages.inShort: A holds a paddle up high as a marker, and B calls the lob and sends it just over, about 60 cm above the paddle.
rules: A stands on the other side of the net at the kitchen line and holds a paddle straight up, as high as possible. That is the height marker.
B calls "lob" first, then lobs. Target: about 60 cm above A's paddle, no higher.
Same stroke as a dink (a soft shot into the kitchen): open paddle face, just more speed. Do not change the technique.
Take the ball as early as you can. The earlier you hit it, the higher it goes on the other side.
Off the bounce, make the motion bigger and get the power from your legs: stand up quickly as you hit.
Aim at A's backhand side. Swap roles after about 5 minutes.
stages.tooEasy: Dink rally with no call: B lobs only when the ball is short or can be taken out of the air, and A may answer with an overhead. Even harder: take the marker away, and A steps back or holds, so B reads it and decides: lob, flick or dink.
stages.tooHard: Lob only when your feet are set. If you still have to move to reach the ball, dink instead.
stages.goodLooksLike: The lob stays low over A's paddle, goes to the backhand side, and only comes off a ball you can attack.

stages.title: Lob Starts the Point
stages.inShort: Dink on half the court until A lobs over B. B answers with an overhead or lets it bounce, then you start again.
rules: Both on one diagonal half of the court. A is the lobber, B defends with the overhead.
B starts with a drop (a soft ball into the kitchen) and moves up to the kitchen line. Then dink, no hard hits.
A looks for the moment to lob over B's head: deep, 60 to 90 cm inside the baseline, not onto the line.
B gets back and hits an overhead (forehand, backhand, or a hook-shot style overhead when running back), or lets the ball bounce and plays a drop. Then start again.
No score, just reps. Aim for about 8 of 10 lobs deep and controlled, and about 7 of 10 overheads down the middle.
Swap roles, and change court spots so each of you plays both roles from both sides.
stages.tooEasy: Play to 11, but a point only counts once a lob has been hit. A lob that works scores 2 points. Even harder: B starts deeper, or A has to call where the lob is going.
stages.tooHard: Stay with no score, and A lobs only over B's backhand shoulder, so B knows where it is coming.
stages.goodLooksLike: Every rally has a lob and an overhead in it, the lobs land deep but in, and the overheads go down the middle.
